newsitem.title: USA: Early Easter boosts discounters, other retailers hurt.
newsitem.headline: Early Easter boosts discounters, other retailers hurt.

text.p: An early Easter boosted candy and general merchandise sales in March at discount retailers reporting Thursday, while cold weather and the loss of a business day due to the holiday hurt some department store chains.

While clothing sales are expected to pick up in April, bolstered by some spring promotions, unseasonably cold weather in some regions could put a damper on retailers' results for this month, analysts said.
Overall, March same-store sales, or sales from stores open at least a year, reported by U.S. retailers Thursday rose between 4 percent and 5 percent, analysts said.
The Salomon Brothers same-store sales index was up 4.4 percent in March, down from the 5.4 percent rise a year ago because of the shift in the Easter holiday to March from April.

"Although most department stores and traditional apparel speciality stores performed poorly, significant strength was seen among the moderate and off-price apparel retailers as well as the discount store operators," Dillon, Read & Co. analyst Peter Schaeffer said in a report.

Because of the early Easter, Salomon Brothers said it believes March and April sales results should be viewed together. Gruntal & Co. brokerage analyst Michael Conn said he expects April same-store sales to approximate March levels.

With Easter on March 30 this year, compared with an April holiday a year ago, some retailers lost a full day of business if they were closed on that Sunday. That cost some retailers as much as two percentage points on their same-stores sales, Conn added.

May Department Stores Co., for example, said its same-store sales for the five-weeks ended April 5 were flat compared with a year ago, which it blamed in part on the loss of one weekend selling day due to Easter Sunday.
The early Easter helped general merchandisers, who saw a jump in sales of candy and other Easter basket goodies.
Kmart Corp. reported a 13 percent jump in same-store sales for its U.S. outlets, which it attributed in part to the early Easter holiday.
Apparel sales, however, did not show the gains that in the past have been associated with Easter.
Cold weather in some parts of the country may have discouraged some shoppers, and analysts noted that consumers do not shop as much for new Easter clothes as they used to.
"We know that Easter is not what it used to be (as an) apparel-driven holiday," Schaeffer said.

The one exception in apparel was seen among moderately priced stores, which continued to attract consumers, analysts noted. For example, Dayton Hudson Corp. said Target, its discount retail chain, saw a 3.5 percent rise in same-store sales, which met the company's plan.

Among other retailers, Sears, Roebuck and Co. reported a 1 percent rise in domestic same-store sales, which followed a 6.8 percent increase a year ago. Sears said it saw strong apparel sales and also benefited from strength in sales of lawn, garden and patio equipment.

Sears stock dropped $3.375 to $47.50 in consolidated afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange. The nation's No. 2 retailer also said Thursday that its 1997 earnings could be hurt by a plan to repay some credit card debtors.
Wal-Mart stock dropped 37.5 cents to $28.25, Dayton Hudson fell 12.5 cents to $42.75, May rose 37.5 cents to $46.375 and Kmart climbed 25 cents to $12.75, all in consolidated NYSE trading.
